In the grey light of a northern port, Solly Two Coats and his crew slipped into a diamond house wearing the rough wool robes of pilgrims. They whispered prayers, heads bowed, until the moment came to crack the strongroom and walk out with a stone the size of a child’s fist. Solly pocketed it and they vanished into the fog.

An ocean away, his cousin Marv got word and sent a terse message: bring the stone straight over. Solly booked passage that same hour. Before he sailed, a scarred man called Grigor the Nail caught him in a dockside tavern and told him of a busy bookmaker’s in the city, a fine place to lay a bet. As Solly nodded along, Grigor quietly sent a second message to a pair of pawnbrokers, Ike and Benno, tipping them to rob Solly at that very address.

Meanwhile, the city’s fight promoters, Halloway and Digby, had a problem. Their fighter Pretty Sam was meant to secure a caravan from a camp of travellers for Coldstone, the gang boss who ran every crooked bout. Halloway and Digby sent Sam to buy it, but a bare-knuckle traveller named Finn took offence at Sam’s manners and knocked him unconscious in the dirt. Now they had no man for Coldstone’s fixed fight. Desperate, Halloway put Finn in Sam’s place and swore to Coldstone that the traveller would go down in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city and went straight to the fence Hersch, who locked the diamond in his safe. Then, following Grigor’s advice, Solly headed for the bookmaker’s to bet on the fight. He barely raised his ticket before Ike, Benno and a third man, Tulley, jumped him in the alley. They were clumsy, shaking hands grabbing at Solly’s case. Solly fought, and in the scuffle they took his arm off at the elbow with a hatchet, seized the case, and ran. Grigor appeared from nowhere, shouting and chasing them off, the picture of a concerned friend.

That night, Finn stepped into the ring and flattened his opponent in the first round with a single blow. Coldstone, watching from ringside, lost a fortune and made sure Halloway felt his displeasure with a broken jaw.

Marv flew in when Solly failed to call. He found only a bloodstained room, and hired a hard-eyed bounty hunter named Ledge to locate his cousin. Ledge began working the streets.

Grigor, meanwhile, had dragged Solly to a cellar. Impatient, he took a bone saw to the handcuff on the severed arm, opened the case, and found nothing but a change of clothes. The stone was not inside. His rage shook the walls.

Ledge was faster than any of them expected. He traced the pawnbrokers, ran their car off the road, and shot the vehicle to scrap. Inside, he found Ike, Benno, and a small strongbox holding the diamond. He took all of it and the two men.

Coldstone had been busy. He fed Solly to his pigs and invited Halloway and Digby to watch the animals eat. He told them exactly what would happen if the next fight didn’t go to plan. So Halloway and Digby cornered Finn and told him to go down in the fourth. When Finn hesitated, Coldstone’s men drove to the traveller camp and set fire to his mother’s caravan while she slept inside.

Grigor, still chasing the stone, ambushed Ledge’s car on a bridge with Ike and Benno still tied in the back seat. Guns came out. In the deafening exchange, Ledge took Grigor through the throat, Benno caught a stray round, and Grigor put two into Ledge’s chest before dropping dead. When the smoke cleared, only Tulley was still breathing. He scrambled from the rear, grabbed a small frightened dog that had been whimpering through it all, and slipped away into the dark. The dog had swallowed the diamond.

At the second fight, Finn climbed into the ring with his mother’s ashes still on his tongue. In the fourth round he looked at Halloway and Digby, then turned and knocked his opponent senseless. Coldstone’s men surged forward, but the travellers were already among the crowd with knives and axes. They took Coldstone’s crew apart in a red minute.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone cowering in his motor and shot him twice. By morning, every traveller had disappeared, their caravans rolled out like a dream.

A week later, a scruffy dog was handed in at a pet shop on the river. It coughed up a diamond in the night. The shop owner, who owed Halloway money, made a call. By noon, Halloway and Digby stood holding the stone, its light catching the dust in the quiet room.

The fluorescent lights of the lymphoma support group hum a frequency that matches my insomnia. I am weeping, and the weeping is a valve, and when the valve closes, I sleep. Then Ada Vey starts attending, her sobs too theatrical, her symptoms recited like a shopping list, and the release stops. I sit dry-eyed and wakeful.

*A window shatters inward, a pressure wave I cannot feel yet. Ada’s hand is in mine, her fingers cold and real. The towers are coming down, and the outside is all orange dust.*

On the redeye to Chicago, the man beside me sells soap. His card says Rex Marrow. He talks about animal fat and lye, and he smells of vetiver. I put the card in my pocket because I am too tired to throw it away.

*My hand is on a workbench, and he holds it there. The lye eats in, a spreading white bloom of pain that flays me open. I try to retreat inside, find the blank space, but he grips my wrist and will not let me go. “Stay,” he says. “You don’t get to leave.”*

I come home from a recall on electric kettles to an address I no longer recognise. The flat is a black mouth, my catalogue furniture blown across the car park. I fumble for the card and dial. Rex answers on the first ring. He takes me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district, where the walls sweat damp and the floors slant.

Outside a bar, he squares up. “Hit me,” he says. “As hard as you can.” I do. His knuckles split my lip open, and the wet sound of it is a lullaby. We beat each other bloody on the tarmac, and it hardens into ritual. A basement, rules, men who bring their own need. We call it the club.

*The car is rolling into oncoming traffic. Rex’s hands are not on the wheel. I grab for it, but the seat beside me is empty and the horn of a truck fills my skull.*

Ada overdoses on something blue, and Rex carries her into the house. She wakes in his cot, and their noise fills all the rooms. I press cushions over my ears. Rex has a new thing by then. He steals liposuction fat from a clinic, cooks it with lye in the basement, and pours it into molds. Eighty dollars a bar at the department stores.

He burns my hand on a Tuesday. I have been inside my head for hours when he locks my fingers and turns the heat on. The pain makes me solid. I cannot float away. The next morning I walk into my employer’s office and let my face do the work. They pay me to stay home.

*The shaven recruits move through the house like a single organism. Havoc, Rex calls it. They wear coveralls and take orders and come back with sledgehammers and spray cans. Corporate towers lose their windows. I watch from the cot, my hand bandaged, my face a foreign thing.*

The car crashes, but Rex is gone. Only the steering wheel and the glass. I sit in the wreck and wait for the sirens.

Ogden dies on an operation, a bullet through the throat. I tell the men to go home, but they look at me with a waiting that frightens. I travel city to city, and in every city I find the same basement club, the same rules, and men who greet me as Rex Marrow. I piece it together slowly, the absences, the blackouts, the way my clothes carry scents I cannot place. Rex is me, acting while I sleep.

Ada is in the kitchen of the derelict house when I return. She doesn’t flinch when I ask. “I’ve been sleeping with you,” she says. “Not a separate man.”

The towers are mined. I find the charges in the subbasement, wires netted through the drywall. I am trying to defuse them when I meet myself at the top of the stairwell. Rex. He beats me down the steps, his fists my fists, his rage my own.

I am on my knees on the concrete, and I put the gun in my mouth. The barrel is cold and tastes of oil. I angle it through my cheek and pull the trigger, and Rex is gone.

The recruits deliver Ada to the tower. She crosses the lobby barefoot and takes my hand at the window. The glass shivers, and outside the sky is filling with ochre light. The charges blow, and we hold on.
